questions.title: The movement that decreases joint angle
questions.question: Which of the following movements decreases the angle between two articulating body segments?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperextension carries a joint beyond its normal extended (straightened) position, further increasing rather than decreasing the angle.
explanations.B: Correct. Flexion is the movement that decreases the angle between two articulating body segments — bending the elbow, for instance, brings the forearm closer to the angle it makes with the arm. Extension is its opposite, increasing that angle back out.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Abduction moves a limb away from the body's midline, a movement on a different axis entirely from the joint-angle change flexion describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adduction moves a limb toward the body's midline — again a different axis from flexion/extension, not a change in joint angle.

questions.learning_objective: Define flexion as the movement decreasing the angle between two articulating segments.

questions.title: Bending a joint to decrease its angle, restated
questions.question: Which movement involves bending the joint to decrease the angle between two body surfaces?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extension is flexion's opposite — it increases the angle between two body segments, straightening the joint rather than bending it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Abduction is movement of a limb away from the body's midline, a separate axis of movement from bending a joint's angle.
explanations.C: Correct. Flexion is the bending movement that decreases the angle between two articulating body segments. It is the term specifically for a joint-angle change, distinct from abduction and adduction, which move a limb relative to the midline rather than change a joint's own angle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adduction is movement of a limb toward the body's midline, again a different axis of movement from bending a joint.

questions.learning_objective: Define flexion as the bending movement decreasing joint angle (restated phrasing).
